rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all 10 compounds, locate their elution window, and identify critical pairs. A 10-minute gradient balances initial separation with the score's preference for early elution.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded early cluster responds to a shallower slope. This also measures the resolution–time tradeoff before adjusting the gradient window or temperature.

Test a substantial temperature increase against injection 1 to shift selectivity in the crowded early cluster while keeping the run short. This will show whether temperature can resolve the near-coelution more efficiently than a shallower gradient.

Keep the favorable high-temperature selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the sole remaining underresolved pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving room to reach the maximum CRF.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to change its selectivity instead. Keep temperature and duration fixed to isolate the gradient-window effect while monitoring the early peaks.

Increase the starting organic fraction one more step, following the improvement in the critical pair from R 1.14 to 1.32. The other pairs have resolution headroom, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Retain injection 6 as the benchmark if either close early pair drops below R 1.5.

Lower the endpoint to make the 8-minute gradient slightly shallower and recover resolution in both close early pairs. The last peak’s estimated elution fraction is about 0.64, so an endpoint of 0.85 should still keep every peak within the gradient.

Test whether another step upward in starting organic fraction can shorten retention while preserving full resolution. Watch the early cluster closely: increasing phi0 helped the previous critical pair but may now compress its neighbors.

Test a one-step temperature decrease against injection 8 to measure the selectivity sensitivity of the two close early pairs. Injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this test may reveal a different balance that permits a steeper gradient.

With maximum CRF already secured, test the opposite temperature limit for an alternative elution order that might resolve the early cluster under a faster gradient. The high endpoint and short gradient should keep the most retained compound within the acquisition window.

Return to the favorable high-temperature selectivity and test a trimmed, 6-minute gradient with a slope between injections 7 and 8. This probes whether full resolution can be retained with a last peak earlier than injection 8.

Injection 12's displayed CRF rounds to 1.000, but its critical pair remains just below full resolution. Lower the endpoint one step to recover separation while retaining a compact gradient; the last peak should elute near the gradient end.

Test whether a shallower gradient can restore the early-pair resolution lost at phi0 0.20 while retaining that window's improved separation of the neighboring pair. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the successful starting fraction and modestly flatten injection 8's gradient to build resolution margin in the critical cluster. This should preserve the maximum CRF with all peaks still comfortably before 10 minutes.

Reduce injection 14's endpoint one step to bring its sole underresolved pair above R 1.5. This tests an alternative fully resolved window while retaining injection 8 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

With maximum CRF already achieved, test a modestly shallower gradient at the successful starting fraction to increase the critical pair's resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Match injection 8's successful gradient slope but end the ramp earlier to test a shorter programmed gradient. The late compounds will elute during the hold, so compare their retention and resolution against injection 8 before accepting this more compact program.

Use an endpoint between injections 8 and 15 to seek a small resolution cushion with less retention-time cost than injection 15. Keeping the late peak inside the gradient avoids the hold-related delay seen in injection 18.

Test the remaining endpoint step between fully resolved injection 8 and faster, slightly underresolved injection 7. This brackets the fastest acceptable 8-minute gradient; retain injection 8 if the critical pair falls below R 1.5.

Back away from the underresolved slope in injection 20 and test a longer version of the fastest fully resolved method. This should retain maximum CRF while providing more separation margin, with the last peak still well before 10 minutes.

Test a shorter programmed gradient in the alternative phi0 0.20 window, with a slope between injections 14 and 16 that may retain full resolution. The final peak may enter the hold, so injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved benchmark.

Trim injection 15 to a 6-minute ramp while preserving its successful slope and early-pair resolution. The endpoint is near the last peak's estimated elution fraction, so this tests whether the shorter program retains maximum CRF without appreciable hold-related delay.

Increase injection 21's endpoint one step to shorten retention while preserving its critical-pair resolution margin. This tests an intermediate speed–resolution compromise between injections 6 and 21; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Use the final injection to test a trimmed endpoint with a slope between fully resolved injections 17 and 21, targeting maximum CRF with additional resolution margin. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with its last peak at 6.04 minutes.
